Founders Fund invests $4m in Gamgee, Rosie the dog’s AI cancer legacy
Date: Sun Aug 23 06:55:00 2026 UTC

The touching tale of puppy love convinced Founders Fund - which raised capital for OpenAI, Spotify, Facebook and Airbnb - to hand $4m in seed funding to Sydney engineer Paul Conyngham to set up a veterinary biotech company named Gamgee. The extraordinary investment - which followed Mr Conyngham's lunch with OpenAI founder Sam Altman - will allow Gamgee to conduct clinical trials on up to 50 more cancer-stricken canines in Australia this year. "I would never have believed in 1000 years that my little dog would have such a huge impact,'' he told The Australian from the US, where he has hired seven staff for his start-up. "It's been a wild ride to get this far. Founders Fund has backed some of the biggest companies on earth. I feel like this is a natural continuation of Rosie's legacy.'' How Sydney tech entrepreneur, Paul Conyngham, used artificial intelligence to create the world's first personalised mRNA cancer vaccine for his rescue dog, achieving remarkable tumour shrinkage that has astounded leading scientists. Founders Fund partner Amin Mirzadegan said he had been impressed by Mr Conyngham's "rare determination''. "What drew us to Paul was his love of Rosie - it led him to teach himself entirely new fields and push forward where most people would have stopped,'' the venture capitalist told The Australian. "That kind of determination is rare, and it's exactly what we look for in a founder. It also speaks to how AI is beginning to push the ball forward on science.'' Mr Conyngham's dogged use of artificial intelligence to devise an experimental cancer treatment for his pet dog Rosie convinced scientists from the University of NSW to help him sequence the DNA in Rosie's tumours to create a personalised mRNA vaccine to treat the dog's mast cell cancer, after chemotherapy had failed. University of Queensland veterinary researcher Professor Rachel Allavena then treated Rosie with the experimental vaccine, using pre-existing ethics approvals. Although the vaccine shrunk Rosie's tumours, she had to be ­euthanised in June at the age of nine, after one tumour grew back aggressively. "The AI extended her life by two years,'' Mr Conyngham said. "We had the cancer relatively contained until that point but something happened that caused the cancer to wake up and become extremely aggressive. "I don't know what happened, but the cancer came back very aggressively post-surgery - it was very sad to see.'' Mr Conyngham has named his start-up company Gamgee, after the Lord of the Rings character Samwise Gamgee - whose wife is named Rosie. He decided it was "an insanely cool name for this company''. So far he has hired seven staff - biologists, coders and marketers - to launch the new vet biotech company. Mr Conyngham said he was negotiating with University of Queensland to gain ethics and regulatory approval to replicate Rosie's treatment in a multi-site clinical trial involving between 30 and 50 dogs stricken with mast cell skin cancer or bone cancer, before the end of this year. He said he hoped to involve veterinarians along the eastern seaboard. Treatment, which would be free for owners, would involve taking a tissue sample from a dog's tumour, sequencing the DNA and then creating a customised immunotherapy treatment for injection back into the dog.

Cats give genetic clues to better cancer treatments (https://www.ft.com/content/807ac68a-d96a-4da0-bdfc-5970c3c5a836)
【turn1064news27】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; A groundbreaking study led by the Wellcome Sanger Institute has revealed that domestic cats share significant genetic similarities with humans in the development of cancer, offering new avenues for treatment in both species. Researchers analyzed 13 types of feline tumors from nearly 500 cats across five countries by sequencing DNA from cancerous and healthy tissues. They found mutations in about 1,000 genes linked to human cancers, across various tumor types like blood, bone, lung, skin, gastrointestinal, and central nervous system cancers.

One key finding relates to feline breast cancer, where over half showed mutations in the FBXW7 gene—rare in humans but linked to worse outcomes. Tests with common chemotherapy drugs such as vincristine and vinorelbine successfully suppressed tumor growth in cat tissues with FBXW7 mutations. This discovery positions felines as potential early test subjects for treatments, especially where human clinical trials are harder to implement.

The research highlights the value of "comparative oncology," studying cancer across species, akin to research on elephants' resistance to tumors. Experts suggest these cross-species studies could offer vital insights into cancer prevention and treatment for humans.
The Wellcome Sanger researchers and colleagues from countries including Canada and Switzerland examined 13 cat cancer types using tissue samples collected by vets from almost 500 domestic animals across five countries. They sequenced DNA from tumours and healthy tissues to look for about 1,000 genes that are associated with cancer in people. The felines showed similar genetic mutations to humans in cases of blood, bone, lung, skin, gastrointestinal and central nervous system tumours.
One of the most intriguing findings was for cat breast cancers, more than half of which showed a mutation in a gene called FBXW7. The change is far rarer in human mammary cancers, but the prognosis for the sufferer is worse when it is present.
The researchers found that the chemotherapeutic drugs vincristine and vinorelbine, used to treat diseases such as leukaemia, curbed the growth of the FBXW7-mutated tumours in cat tissues. 
This suggested an initial test of the drugs' effectiveness against breast cancer could be done in felines, as a trial in people would be hard to organise because of the FBXW7 mutation's relative scarcity.
"Since vincristine is already in use in both human and veterinary clinics, it offers the opportunity for use in a clinical trial in felines with mammary cancer, with the results being extremely informative for human breast cancer patients," said Louise Van Der Weyden, a cancer genetics expert at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and senior author of the cat paper.
The feline cancer work was an interesting contribution to the expanding field of "comparative oncology" between humans and other animals, said Trevor Graham, professor of genomics and evolution at The Institute of Cancer Research, London.
Other researchers are examining whether the suspected genetic reasons for elephants' striking resistance to malignant tumours can be translated into treatments for humans.  
"Understanding the mechanisms that make different species better - or worse - at suppressing cancer may give us clues about how to prevent or treat human disease," Graham said. 
"Humans and animals have a shared evolutionary history, so there is much we can potentially learn by studying cancers in other animals that could eventually benefit human patients - and vice versa."

Your Next Dog May Live Longer (https://www.theatlantic.com/science/2026/05/celine-halioua-loyal-pet-longevity/687005/?utm_source=apple_news)
【turn1064news28】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 5 months ago; Celine Halioua, the 31-year-old founder of Loyal, a biotech company focused on canine longevity, has developed a pill that could extend dogs' lives by addressing insulin sensitivity. Approved as “likely effective” by the FDA in early 2025, Loyal's pill represents a shift toward treating aging itself rather than just organ-specific diseases. The pill, designed to boost insulin response and combat age-related diseases like cancer and heart decline, is expected to cost around $100/month and may reach the market soon, pending full regulatory approval.

Driven by her personal attachment to animals and her professional background in genetics and longevity research, Halioua chose to start with dogs for both scientific and emotional reasons. Dogs age similarly to humans, making them useful models for potential human applications. Her company has launched a five-year clinical trial involving 1,300 dogs to validate the pill's efficacy.

The broader implications of dog life-extension include potential shifts in human-animal relationships and ethical questions about affordability and euthanasia. Loyal’s success could eventually pave the way for similar treatments in human longevity. Halioua hopes to use the profits from the drug to fund future human aging research without relying on large pharmaceutical companies.
Above a certain socioeconomic threshold, not spending an extra $1,000 a year or more in the hopes of doing so could seem neglectful. Elderly people may think twice about adopting dogs that have the potential to live much longer. Euthanasia decisions are already brutalizing for dog owners, and those decisions may become even more fraught. 
The fundamental sadness of loving a dog is knowing that you are more likely to lose them than vice versa, because their lifespan is easily contained by yours. There's every reason to try to keep them around longer, especially if the extra years are healthy ones. But our relationship with them may change if we succeed, perhaps in some ways that we don't expect. 
Loyal's clinical trial, which the company says is the largest one ever run on an animal drug, began in December 2023. More than 1,300 dogs enrolled, all at least 10 years old and weighing at least 14 pounds, and representing many different breeds. Age verification at times proved difficult; some owners submitted screenshots of Facebook posts they'd made back when the dogs were puppies. Most clinical trials for dogs last a month or two, but the owners of these dogs have committed to keeping at it for at least half a decade. They don't even know whether their pet might be taking a placebo, as half of the test population is. The FDA expects the pill to be safe, but no dog has yet had it in their system for five years. 
By the time the trial finishes, Halioua may already have had the drug on the market for years. She recently assembled a focus group of 20 taste-tester dogs to get the flavor just right at launch.
